title: 1. What SQL Is: Tables, Rows, Keys & How Queries Run
summary:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is how you talk to a relational database. A relational database stores data in tables, and a table is just a grid, like a spreadsheet: each column has a name and a type (INT, VARCHAR, DATE...), and each row is one record. A table called Employees might have columns id, name, salary, and department_id, and every row is one actual employee. Two ideas make tables 'relational': a primary key is a column (often id) whose value uniquely identifies each row, and a foreign key is a column in one table that holds the primary key of a row in another table. That is how an Orders row 'points at' the Customers row that placed it, without copying the customer's data into every order.

The most important mindset shift: SQL is declarative. You do not write loops that walk over rows; you describe the result you want, and the database engine figures out how to produce it. Your whole job is to describe the correct set of rows and columns.

Even though you WRITE a query starting with SELECT, the database LOGICALLY runs the clauses in this order: FROM (get the tables and join them) -> WHERE (throw away rows that fail the condition) -> GROUP BY (collapse surviving rows into buckets) -> HAVING (throw away whole buckets) -> SELECT (compute the output columns) -> ORDER BY (sort the results) -> LIMIT (keep only the first N). Burn this order into memory, because it explains almost every 'weird' SQL error. For example: WHERE runs before SELECT, so a column alias you invent in SELECT does not exist yet when WHERE runs, and WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so WHERE can never see an aggregate like COUNT(*). Beginners who memorize the writing order instead of the execution order fight the language forever; those who learn the execution order can predict what is legal without memorizing rules.

examples.description: A tiny Employees table (id, name, salary, department_id) is created so we have something to query. In interviews you rarely write DDL, but reading it tells you the column types and which column is the primary key.
examples.explanation: This works because CREATE TABLE declares the grid before any data exists: each line names a column and its type, and PRIMARY KEY promises that no two rows will ever share an id. Knowing which column is the primary key matters later — it is the column you join on, and the reason 'one row per id' is a safe assumption in every query you write against this table.

examples.description: Read every column of every row from Employees — the 'hello world' of SQL.
examples.query:
SELECT *
FROM Employees;
examples.explanation: FROM runs first and loads the Employees table; SELECT then decides which columns to output, and * means 'all of them'. There is no WHERE, so no rows are filtered — you get the entire table back. In real code you should list columns explicitly instead of *, because * silently changes meaning when someone adds a column to the table.

examples.description: From the same Employees table, output only each employee's name and salary, renaming salary to annual_salary.
examples.query:
SELECT name, salary AS annual_salary
FROM Employees;
examples.explanation: This works because SELECT is a projection step: after FROM has produced the rows, SELECT picks just the name and salary columns and throws the rest away. AS gives the output column a new header. The alias exists only in the OUTPUT — which is exactly why the next example fails when it tries to filter on it.

examples.description: A classic beginner error, shown on purpose: try to filter Employees using the alias defined in SELECT. MySQL rejects this with 'Unknown column annual_salary'.
examples.query:
SELECT name, salary AS annual_salary
FROM Employees
WHERE annual_salary > 50000;  -- ERROR! Use: WHERE salary > 50000
examples.explanation: This fails precisely because of logical execution order: WHERE runs BEFORE SELECT, so at the moment WHERE evaluates each row, the name annual_salary has not been created yet — only the real column salary exists. The fix is to repeat the real expression (WHERE salary > 50000). Contrast: ORDER BY runs AFTER SELECT, so ORDER BY annual_salary would be perfectly legal. One rule, two behaviors, both predicted by the execution order.

examples.description: A full pipeline on Employees: departments (department_id) whose average salary exceeds 60000, highest average first, top 3 only. Every clause of the execution order appears once.
examples.query:
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM Employees
WHERE salary > 0
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > 60000
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC
LIMIT 3;
examples.explanation: Trace it in execution order and every clause makes sense: FROM loads all employees; WHERE discards bad rows (salary 0) while they are still individual rows; GROUP BY collapses the survivors into one bucket per department_id; HAVING discards whole buckets whose AVG(salary) is too low — it must be HAVING, not WHERE, because the average only exists after grouping; SELECT computes the two output columns; ORDER BY sorts those results (it may use the alias, since SELECT already ran); LIMIT keeps the top 3. If you can narrate a query like this, you understand SQL's engine — everything else in the course is vocabulary.

title: 2. SELECT, WHERE & Operators (comparison, AND/OR/NOT, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE)
summary:
WHERE is your row filter: the database checks the condition against every row, one at a time, and keeps only the rows where the condition is TRUE. The condition is built from comparison operators — = (equal), <> or != (not equal), <, <=, >, >= — and every one of them produces TRUE or FALSE for a row (or UNKNOWN when NULLs are involved, which gets its own lesson next). Note that SQL uses a single = for comparison, not ==, and string literals go in single quotes: name = 'Alice'.

You combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT, and here lives the number one beginner bug: AND binds tighter than OR, exactly like multiplication binds tighter than addition. The condition a = 1 OR a = 2 AND b = 3 means a = 1 OR (a = 2 AND b = 3), which is almost never what you meant. The cure is simple: the moment a WHERE mixes AND with OR, wrap the OR part in parentheses. Interviewers genuinely test this.

Three shorthands make conditions readable. IN checks membership in a list: country IN ('USA', 'Canada') is the same as two = checks joined with OR, but scales cleanly and later accepts a subquery. BETWEEN checks a range and is INCLUSIVE on both ends: x BETWEEN 5 AND 10 means x >= 5 AND x <= 10 — remember the inclusivity, it is a favorite off-by-one trap with dates. LIKE does pattern matching on strings: % matches any run of characters (including none) and _ matches exactly one character, so name LIKE 'A%' finds names starting with A, and name LIKE '_a%' finds names whose SECOND letter is a. LIKE with a leading % ('%gmail.com') works but cannot use an index — fine for interviews, worth knowing for the 'how would this scale?' follow-up.

examples.description: From a Products table (product_id, name, price, category), find products cheaper than 20.
examples.explanation: The engine walks every row of Products, evaluates price < 20 for that row, and keeps the row only when the comparison is TRUE. This 'one row at a time, keep on TRUE' picture is the correct mental model for every WHERE you will ever write — no matter how complicated the condition gets, it always reduces to a per-row TRUE/FALSE verdict.

examples.description: LeetCode-style (Big Countries): from a World table (name, continent, area, population), find countries that are big by area (>= 3,000,000) OR by population (>= 25,000,000).
examples.query:
SELECT name, population, area
FROM World
WHERE area >= 3000000
   OR population >= 25000000;
examples.explanation: OR keeps a row if EITHER condition is TRUE, so a huge-area country with a small population still qualifies — that is exactly the problem's definition of 'big'. Using AND here would silently demand BOTH conditions and return far fewer rows; choosing between AND and OR by re-reading the English requirement ('either... or...') is the actual skill being tested.

examples.description: From an Orders table (order_id, customer_id, status, amount), find orders that are shipped or delivered AND worth more than 100 — demonstrating why parentheses are mandatory when mixing OR with AND.
examples.query:
SELECT order_id, status, amount
FROM Orders
WHERE (status = 'shipped' OR status = 'delivered')
  AND amount > 100;
examples.explanation: Without the parentheses, MySQL would parse this as status = 'shipped' OR (status = 'delivered' AND amount > 100) because AND binds tighter than OR — and every shipped order would leak through regardless of amount. The parentheses force the intended grouping: first decide 'is it shipped or delivered?', then require the amount check on top. Whenever AND and OR share a WHERE, parenthesize; it costs nothing and prevents the most common silent-wrong-answer bug in SQL.

examples.description: Same Orders table: rewrite the status check with IN, and add a date range with BETWEEN on an order_date column.
examples.query:
SELECT order_id, status, amount
FROM Orders
WHERE status IN ('shipped', 'delivered')
  AND order_date BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31';
examples.explanation: IN succeeds when the row's status equals ANY value in the list — it is exactly the parenthesized OR from the previous example, compressed into one readable test, which is why no extra parentheses are needed. BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends, so orders placed ON Jan 1 and ON Jan 31 are both kept. One care point with DATETIME columns: '2026-01-31' means midnight starting that day, so a timestamp of 2026-01-31 09:00 would be EXCLUDED — with timestamps, prefer order_date >= '2026-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-02-01'.

examples.description: From a Users table (user_id, name, mail), find users whose mail is on the leetcode.com domain and starts with a letter prefix — a simplified version of LeetCode's 'Find Users With Valid E-Mails'.
examples.explanation: LIKE compares the string against a template: % absorbs any prefix (the account name), and the literal tail '@leetcode.com' must match exactly, so only that domain passes. This works because LIKE anchors the pattern to the WHOLE string — the mail must END with the literal part since nothing follows the pattern. If you needed 'second character is a', you would use '_a%': _ consumes exactly one character, % the rest. When patterns get more complex than % and _ can express (character classes, repetition), MySQL's REGEXP takes over — LIKE is the 90% tool, REGEXP the escape hatch.

examples.description: Interview-level combination on a Patients table (patient_id, patient_name, conditions), where conditions is a space-separated list of codes: find patients with Type I Diabetes, whose codes start with the prefix DIAB1 (LeetCode 1527 pattern).
examples.query:
SELECT patient_id, patient_name, conditions
FROM Patients
WHERE conditions LIKE 'DIAB1%'
   OR conditions LIKE '% DIAB1%';
examples.explanation: The tricky part is that DIAB1 must start a CODE, not merely appear anywhere — 'ADIAB1' must not match. Two patterns cover the only two legal positions: 'DIAB1%' matches when the very first code has the prefix, and '% DIAB1%' matches when the prefix appears immediately after a space, i.e. starts a later code in the list. A naive single '%DIAB1%' would also match text where DIAB1 sits inside another word, which is exactly the wrong answer graders check for. This is how real interview LIKE questions work: the pattern encodes a POSITION rule, not just a substring.

title: 3. NULL: The Three-Valued Logic Trap
summary:
NULL is not a value — it is the ABSENCE of a value, a marker meaning 'unknown' or 'not applicable'. That single idea explains all of NULL's strange behavior. Because NULL means 'unknown', any comparison with it yields neither TRUE nor FALSE but a third truth value: UNKNOWN. NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN (are two unknown things equal? who knows). NULL <> 5 is UNKNOWN too. And here is the trap that breaks beginners' queries: WHERE keeps a row only when the condition is TRUE — UNKNOWN rows are dropped just like FALSE ones. So WHERE referee_id <> 2 silently drops every row where referee_id is NULL, even though 'not 2' feels like it should include them. This exact trap IS LeetCode 584 (Find Customer Referee), one of the first Top-50 problems.

To test for NULL you must use the special operators IS NULL and IS NOT NULL — they are the only comparisons that give a definite TRUE/FALSE answer on NULL. To REPLACE a NULL with a default, MySQL gives you IFNULL(x, fallback) (two arguments) and the standard COALESCE(a, b, c, ...) which returns the first non-NULL argument in the list. COALESCE is the more general tool and works on every database.

Two more places NULL bites. First, aggregates: COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX all IGNORE NULLs — AVG(salary) divides by the number of non-NULL salaries, not the number of rows, which is sometimes exactly what you want and sometimes a subtle bug. Only COUNT(*) counts every row. Second, NOT IN: if the list produced by a subquery contains even one NULL, x NOT IN (list) can never be TRUE for any x (because x <> NULL is UNKNOWN, and one UNKNOWN poisons the AND-chain), so the query returns zero rows with no error. That silent failure is a famous senior-level gotcha — the fixes are filtering NULLs out of the subquery or using NOT EXISTS.

examples.description: From an Employees table (id, name, manager_id), find employees who have no manager — the manager_id is NULL for them.
examples.explanation: IS NULL is the only correct test here. Writing manager_id = NULL would return zero rows — not because no one lacks a manager, but because = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN for every single row, and WHERE discards UNKNOWN. IS NULL exists precisely to sidestep three-valued logic: it directly asks 'is this cell empty?' and answers a plain TRUE or FALSE.

examples.description: LeetCode 584 (Find Customer Referee): from Customer (id, name, referee_id), find customers NOT referred by customer 2. Customers with no referrer (NULL) must be included.
examples.query:
SELECT name
FROM Customer
WHERE referee_id <> 2
   OR referee_id IS NULL;
examples.explanation: The naive WHERE referee_id <> 2 fails because for a NULL referee_id the comparison is UNKNOWN, so those rows are dropped even though 'nobody referred them' clearly satisfies 'not referred by 2' in plain English. The OR referee_id IS NULL branch rescues exactly those rows: each row now passes if the comparison is definitively TRUE or the cell is empty. This one-line fix is the canonical demonstration that SQL logic and English logic disagree about NULL — expect a variant of it in nearly every SQL screen.

examples.description: From a Sales table (sale_id, product_id, bonus), display each sale with its bonus, showing 0 instead of NULL when no bonus was recorded.
examples.query:
SELECT sale_id, IFNULL(bonus, 0) AS bonus
FROM Sales;
examples.explanation: IFNULL(bonus, 0) evaluates bonus for the current row; if it is a real value it passes through untouched, and only when it is NULL does the fallback 0 appear. This works because IFNULL is an ordinary per-row function running in the SELECT phase — it rewrites the OUTPUT without touching the stored data. COALESCE(bonus, 0) is the portable spelling; prefer it when you might ever run the query outside MySQL, or when you want a chain of fallbacks like COALESCE(nickname, full_name, 'anonymous').

examples.description: LeetCode 176-style (Second Highest Salary): from Employee (id, salary), return the second highest DISTINCT salary — and return NULL (not an empty result) when it does not exist.
examples.explanation: The inner query finds the answer: DISTINCT collapses duplicate salaries, ORDER BY ... DESC ranks them, and LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 skips the highest and takes the next. The clever part is WHY it is wrapped in an outer SELECT: if the table has fewer than two distinct salaries, the inner query returns NO ROWS — but the problem demands a row containing NULL. A scalar subquery that produces no row evaluates to NULL, so the wrapper converts 'empty result' into 'one row holding NULL' for free. Here NULL's 'absence of a value' semantics are used deliberately as a feature, not suffered as a bug.

examples.description: The NOT IN + NULL trap, shown on purpose: from Customers (id, name) and Orders (order_id, customer_id), find customers who never ordered — but the Orders table contains a row whose customer_id is NULL.
examples.query:
SELECT name
FROM Customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM Orders);  -- returns 0 rows!
-- Fix: ... NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM Orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL)
examples.explanation: NOT IN expands to a chain of inequalities: id <> o1 AND id <> o2 AND ... AND id <> NULL. That last term is UNKNOWN for every id, and TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, so the whole condition is never TRUE and the query silently returns nothing — no error, no warning. The fix in the comment excludes NULLs from the subquery so every inequality can resolve; the more robust alternative is NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id), which handles NULLs correctly by construction. Interviewers love this because the broken query LOOKS obviously right.

examples.description: Aggregates ignoring NULL: a Ratings table (user_id, stars) where some users have not rated yet (stars IS NULL). Compare row count, rating count, and the average.
examples.query:
SELECT COUNT(*)          AS all_rows,
       COUNT(stars)      AS rated_rows,
       ROUND(AVG(stars), 2) AS avg_stars
FROM Ratings;
examples.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of content, COUNT(stars) counts only rows where stars IS NOT NULL, and AVG(stars) computes SUM of the non-NULL stars divided by COUNT(stars) — the NULL rows are invisible to it. That is usually right ('average among people who rated') but becomes a bug if the requirement is 'average treating no-rating as zero'; then you must write AVG(IFNULL(stars, 0)) to force the NULLs into the calculation. Being able to say which of the two averages a question is asking for is exactly what separates a memorized answer from understanding.

title: 4. DISTINCT, ORDER BY & LIMIT/OFFSET
summary:
These three tools shape the final result set, and by execution order they all run late: SELECT computes the output columns, DISTINCT then removes duplicate output rows, ORDER BY sorts what is left, and LIMIT/OFFSET cuts a window out of the sorted list.

DISTINCT deduplicates ENTIRE OUTPUT ROWS, not individual columns. SELECT DISTINCT city gives each city once; SELECT DISTINCT city, state gives each (city, state) COMBINATION once — a common misreading is thinking DISTINCT 'applies to' the column it happens to sit next to. It does not; it applies to the whole row the SELECT produces. Also note DISTINCT treats all NULLs as one group, so one NULL survives deduplication.

ORDER BY sorts by one or more keys: ORDER BY salary DESC, name ASC means 'sort by salary high-to-low, and break ties alphabetically by name'. Each key gets its own ASC (default) or DESC. Because ORDER BY runs after SELECT, it is the one clause allowed to use your column aliases. In MySQL, NULLs sort FIRST under ASC and LAST under DESC — remember that when a sorted column is nullable. Without an ORDER BY, row order is NOT guaranteed, ever; if the problem says 'return in any order' you may skip it, otherwise it is mandatory.

LIMIT n keeps the first n rows of the sorted result; LIMIT n OFFSET m skips m rows first, then keeps n. This pair powers pagination (page 3 of 10-per-page = LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20) and, crucially for interviews, Nth-highest problems: the 2nd highest distinct salary is ORDER BY salary DESC with LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 — but only if you deduplicate salaries FIRST, otherwise two people tied at the top make the 'second row' just another copy of the highest value. LIMIT without ORDER BY is meaningless — you are asking for 'any n rows'.

examples.description: From a Customers table (customer_id, name, city), list each city that has at least one customer, once.
examples.query:
SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM Customers;
examples.explanation: Without DISTINCT you would get the city repeated once per customer living there. DISTINCT works by comparing complete output rows after SELECT builds them and keeping one representative of each duplicate group — here the output row is just (city), so each city survives exactly once. Note it deduplicates the RESULT, not the table: Customers itself is untouched.

examples.description: From an Orders table (order_id, customer_id, product_id), find the distinct (customer_id, product_id) pairs — who has ever bought what — showing that DISTINCT covers the whole row.
examples.query:
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, product_id
FROM Orders;
examples.explanation: A customer who bought product 7 three times contributes one (customer, 7) row, but the SAME customer buying product 9 still appears again with 9 — because DISTINCT keeps every unique combination of ALL selected columns, not unique values of the first column. Misreading this as 'distinct customer_id, and also show product_id' is a classic mistake; if you truly want one row per customer you need GROUP BY customer_id and must decide which product to show via an aggregate.

examples.description: From Employees (id, name, salary, hire_date), list everyone sorted by salary high-to-low, with alphabetical name as the tiebreaker.
examples.explanation: Multiple sort keys work like dictionary ordering: rows are compared by the first key, and ONLY when salaries tie does the second key decide. Each key carries its own direction — DESC on salary, ASC on name — a detail beginners miss by writing ORDER BY salary, name DESC and accidentally sorting salary ascending. Deterministic tiebreakers matter in graded problems: if two employees tie and the expected output has them alphabetical, omitting the second key can fail the test even though your 'main' sort was right.

examples.description: Pagination over a Products table (product_id, name, price): show page 3 of the catalog, 10 products per page, cheapest first.
examples.query:
SELECT product_id, name, price
FROM Products
ORDER BY price ASC, product_id ASC
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;
examples.explanation: OFFSET 20 skips pages 1 and 2 (2 pages x 10 rows), then LIMIT 10 takes exactly page 3 — the arithmetic is OFFSET = (page - 1) * page_size. This only works because ORDER BY makes the row sequence stable and product_id breaks price ties: without a total order, the database could legally return DIFFERENT rows for the same page on each run, causing items to duplicate or vanish as a user flips pages. 'LIMIT/OFFSET require a deterministic ORDER BY' is the rule; mentioning that huge OFFSETs get slow (the engine still walks the skipped rows) earns scaling points in interviews.

examples.description: LeetCode 176/177 pattern (Nth Highest Salary): from Employee (id, salary), fetch the 2nd highest DISTINCT salary, handling ties correctly.
examples.explanation: The three clauses each defeat one failure mode. DISTINCT defeats ties: with salaries 300, 300, 200, skipping one ROW would land on the duplicate 300, but skipping one distinct VALUE correctly lands on 200. ORDER BY salary DESC establishes the ranking that makes 'offset 1' MEAN 'second highest'. LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 selects exactly that value. The outer SELECT wrapper handles the final edge: with fewer than two distinct salaries the inner query is empty, and an empty scalar subquery yields NULL — matching the required 'return NULL if absent'. Every clause here answers a specific 'but what if...' — that is what interview-grade SQL looks like.

title: 5. Aggregate Functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
summary:
An aggregate function collapses MANY rows into ONE value: COUNT how many, SUM the total, AVG the mean, MIN/MAX the extremes. Without a GROUP BY (next lesson), an aggregate treats the entire filtered table as one big group and the query returns exactly one row. The mental model: WHERE first decides which rows participate, then the aggregate folds them into a single number.

The distinction interviewers probe first: COUNT(*) counts ROWS — every row, no exceptions. COUNT(col) counts rows where col IS NOT NULL. COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values. Three different questions, three different answers on the same table. The same NULL rule applies to all aggregates: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX skip NULLs entirely, so AVG(bonus) is the average among people who HAVE a bonus, not across everyone — if you need NULL to count as zero, write AVG(IFNULL(bonus, 0)). And on an empty set of rows, COUNT returns 0 but SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX return NULL — a difference that matters whenever a query might match nothing.

Presentation: AVG in MySQL happily produces long decimals; problems almost always demand ROUND(expr, 2). Money sums use ROUND too.

Finally, the trick that unlocks a whole family of Top-50 problems — conditional aggregation. In MySQL a boolean comparison evaluates to 1 (true) or 0 (false), so SUM(status = 'late') counts late rows, and AVG(status = 'late') IS the fraction of late rows, ready to multiply by 100 for a percentage. The portable spelling is SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'late' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). Either way, the insight is the same: you can count a SUBSET of a group without a second query, by turning the condition into a 0/1 number and aggregating that.

examples.description: From an Orders table (order_id, customer_id, amount, coupon_code), count how many orders exist in total.
examples.query:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders
FROM Orders;
examples.explanation: COUNT(*) asks 'how many rows survived the (absent) WHERE?' and since nothing was filtered, it counts the whole table. The * here does NOT mean 'all columns' the way it does in SELECT * — it means 'the row itself', so no column's NULLness can affect the tally. With no GROUP BY, the entire table is one implicit group, which is why the result is a single row.

examples.description: Same Orders table: compare COUNT(*), COUNT(coupon_code), and COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) — three counts, three meanings.
examples.query:
SELECT COUNT(*)                    AS total_orders,
       COUNT(coupon_code)          AS orders_with_coupon,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers
FROM Orders;
examples.explanation: All three scan the same rows but ask different questions. COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(coupon_code) skips rows where coupon_code IS NULL, so it counts orders that USED a coupon — the NULL-skipping is a feature being exploited, not an accident. COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) first deduplicates the non-NULL customer_ids, then counts, answering 'how many different customers ordered?'. Reading a requirement and picking the right one of these three is a genuine screening question; saying 'count' without deciding which count is how wrong answers happen.

examples.description: From an Employees table (id, name, salary), get the lowest, highest, and average salary, with the average rounded to 2 decimals.
examples.query:
SELECT MIN(salary)            AS lowest,
       MAX(salary)            AS highest,
       ROUND(AVG(salary), 2)  AS average
FROM Employees;
examples.explanation: Multiple aggregates can share one query because each independently folds the same set of rows — one pass computes all three. ROUND wraps AVG because AVG returns a high-precision decimal (e.g. 64333.333333) and graders compare output EXACTLY: an unrounded average is marked wrong even though it is mathematically correct. ROUND(x, 2) is applied in the SELECT phase, after the aggregate value exists — you are rounding the final number, not each salary.

examples.description: LeetCode 1251 pattern (Average Selling Price flavor): from a Sales table (product_id, price, units), compute total revenue per query run and the weighted average price, guarding a possible empty table.
examples.explanation: SUM(price * units) works because the expression inside an aggregate is computed PER ROW first (each row's revenue) and the aggregate then folds those products — aggregates accept arbitrary expressions, not just bare columns. The weighted average must be SUM(price*units)/SUM(units), not AVG(price): AVG would weight a 1-unit sale equally with a 1000-unit sale. IFNULL guards the empty-set behavior — SUM over zero rows is NULL, not 0, and division involving NULL stays NULL — converting 'no data' into the 0 the problem expects. This exact NULL-on-empty guard is what separates accepted from wrong-answer on several Top-50 problems.

examples.description: Conditional aggregation, MySQL idiom: from a Deliveries table (delivery_id, order_date, customer_pref_date), find the percentage of 'immediate' orders (ordered and preferred same day) — LeetCode 1173.
examples.query:
SELECT ROUND(AVG(order_date = customer_pref_date) * 100, 2) AS immediate_percentage
FROM Deliveries;
examples.explanation: The comparison order_date = customer_pref_date is evaluated per row and, in MySQL, yields 1 or 0. AVG of a column of 1s and 0s is (number of 1s) / (total rows) — literally the definition of 'fraction of rows satisfying the condition'. Multiply by 100 and round, and the percentage falls out of ONE aggregate with no subquery, no CASE, no join. This works only because MySQL treats booleans as numbers; the portable equivalent is AVG(CASE WHEN order_date = customer_pref_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). Knowing both forms, and why they are the same, is a strong interview signal.

examples.description: Two counts with different filters in ONE query: from a Trips table (id, status, request_date), count total trips and cancelled trips per the whole table using SUM over a condition.
examples.explanation: The naive route is two separate queries (or a subquery per count); conditional aggregation does both in one scan. CASE converts each row into a 1 if it matches the cancellation condition, else 0, and SUM adds those up — a count of a SUBSET, computed inside a query that still sees the WHOLE set. This composability is the point: you can compute five differently-filtered counts side by side, which is exactly the shape of cancellation-rate and acceptance-rate problems (LeetCode 262, 1211). WHERE could not do this, because WHERE removes rows for ALL aggregates at once.

title: 6. GROUP BY & HAVING (grouping mental model, HAVING vs WHERE)
summary:
GROUP BY turns 'one number for the whole table' into 'one number PER CATEGORY'. The mental model: after FROM and WHERE have produced the surviving rows, GROUP BY deals them into buckets — one bucket per distinct value of the grouping column(s) — and then every aggregate in the query runs once per bucket. The output has exactly one row per bucket. GROUP BY department_id, one row per department; GROUP BY customer_id, product_id, one row per (customer, product) pair.

The iron rule of grouped queries: once you group, each output row REPRESENTS many rows, so SELECT may only mention (a) the grouping columns — constant within a bucket, safe to print — or (b) aggregates, which fold the bucket into one value. Selecting any other bare column (SELECT name ... GROUP BY department_id) is asking 'which single name represents fifty employees?' — an unanswerable question. Modern MySQL (ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, on by default) rejects it as an error; old MySQL picked an arbitrary value, which was worse. If you need 'the row with the max value per group', that is a different pattern (join or subquery against the per-group max), not a bare column.

HAVING is WHERE for buckets. WHERE runs BEFORE grouping and filters individual rows; it cannot contain aggregates because no bucket exists yet. HAVING runs AFTER grouping and filters whole buckets; it is the only place a condition like COUNT(*) > 1 or SUM(amount) >= 1000 can live. The decision rule is one question: does the condition need a per-group total to be computed first? If yes, HAVING; if it can be checked on a single row, WHERE — and putting it in WHERE is strictly better, because rows removed early never waste grouping work. Using both in one query is normal and common: WHERE to discard irrelevant rows, GROUP BY to bucket, HAVING to keep only interesting buckets.

examples.description: From an Employees table (id, name, department_id, salary), count employees per department.
examples.explanation: GROUP BY department_id deals every employee row into a bucket keyed by department, and COUNT(*) then runs once per bucket, counting its rows. The SELECT list is legal because it contains only the grouping column (identical for every row in a bucket, so unambiguous to print) and an aggregate. One output row per department — if the query returns 5 rows, the company has 5 distinct department_id values among its employees.

examples.description: LeetCode 182 (Duplicate Emails): from a Person table (id, email), report every email that appears more than once.
examples.query:
SELECT email
FROM Person
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
examples.explanation: Grouping by email puts all rows sharing an address into one bucket, so COUNT(*) per bucket IS that email's number of occurrences. The condition must be HAVING, not WHERE: WHERE runs before grouping, when each row is alone and 'appears more than once' is not yet a computable fact about it. HAVING runs after the buckets exist and discards those with count 1. This tiny query is the archetype of a whole problem family — 'find groups whose aggregate passes a threshold' — and recognizing that shape is the skill.

examples.description: WHERE and HAVING cooperating: from an Orders table (order_id, customer_id, amount, status), find customers whose COMPLETED orders total at least 1000.
examples.query:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_spent
FROM Orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 1000;
examples.explanation: The two filters do different jobs at different times. WHERE status = 'completed' is a per-row fact, so it runs first and keeps cancelled orders out of the buckets entirely — putting it in HAVING instead would be impossible to even express correctly, because after grouping there is no single 'status' per customer. HAVING SUM(amount) >= 1000 is a per-bucket fact that can only be checked once each customer's completed total exists. Swapping the placement of these conditions is the classic exam trap; the tell is always 'can a single row answer this?'.

examples.description: Grouping by two columns: from a Sales table (sale_id, product_id, region, units), get units sold per product per region.
examples.explanation: With two grouping columns, a bucket is a distinct (product_id, region) COMBINATION — product 7 in 'EU' and product 7 in 'US' are different buckets, so a product appears in as many output rows as regions it sold in. This works because the bucket key is the tuple, and both key parts are constant inside their bucket, making both safe to SELECT. Choosing the grouping columns is choosing the granularity of your answer: the question 'per X per Y' translates mechanically into GROUP BY X, Y.

examples.description: The illegal query, shown on purpose: try to display each department's highest-paid employee's NAME with a bare column. MySQL rejects it under ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY.
examples.query:
SELECT department_id, name, MAX(salary)
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department_id;  -- ERROR: 'name' not in GROUP BY and not aggregated
examples.explanation: The query fails because a bucket holds MANY employees, and while MAX(salary) folds their salaries into one value, name has no fold — MySQL would have to pick one of fifty names arbitrarily, and the name it picked would NOT necessarily belong to the max-salary row. That mismatch (people assume the bare column comes from the same row as the MAX — it does not, and cannot) caused years of silent bugs before ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY made it an error. The correct pattern computes each department's max first, then joins back: WHERE (department_id, salary) IN (SELECT department_id, MAX(salary) FROM Employees GROUP BY department_id) — 'find the row matching the per-group extreme', which is LeetCode 184's exact shape.

examples.description: Interview-level (LeetCode 596 flavor): from a Courses table (student, class), find classes with at least 5 DISTINCT students, defending against duplicate enrollment rows.
examples.query:
SELECT class
FROM Courses
GROUP BY class
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT student) >= 5;
examples.explanation: Grouping by class buckets the enrollments, and COUNT(DISTINCT student) measures each bucket's UNIQUE student count — the DISTINCT matters because a duplicated (student, class) row would otherwise inflate plain COUNT(*) and let a 4-student class sneak over the threshold. HAVING then keeps only qualifying buckets. This is the finished form of the grouping pattern: pick the grouping key from the phrase 'per class', pick the aggregate from 'number of students', pick DISTINCT from asking 'can the same student appear twice?', and put the threshold in HAVING because it tests the group. Every grouped interview question decomposes into those four decisions.

title: 7. JOINs Part 1: INNER & LEFT JOIN
summary:
Real data is split across tables — customers here, their orders there, connected by a key. JOIN is how you recombine them. The mental model for A JOIN B ON condition: for EACH row of A, scan B for rows where the ON condition is TRUE, and output one combined row (all of A's columns + all of B's columns) per match. One A-row matching three B-rows produces three output rows; matching zero produces — and here the join types split.

INNER JOIN keeps only matched combinations; an A-row with no partner in B simply vanishes from the output. LEFT JOIN keeps EVERY row of the left table no matter what: when no B-row matches, the A-row still comes out once, with all of B's columns filled with NULL. A text picture, joining Customers to Orders on customer id — Alice(1) has orders O1 and O2, Bob(2) has none:

INNER: Alice+O1, Alice+O2. (Bob vanishes.)
LEFT:  Alice+O1, Alice+O2, Bob+NULL. (Bob survives, padded with NULLs.)

Choose by asking: 'must rows WITHOUT a match still appear?' If yes, LEFT JOIN with the must-keep table on the left. Those NULL-padded rows are also a query tool: WHERE b.key IS NULL after a LEFT JOIN isolates exactly the left rows that had NO match — the standard 'customers who never ordered' pattern (LeetCode 183).

The subtle trap: with LEFT JOIN, a filter on the RIGHT table placed in WHERE destroys the LEFT-ness. LEFT JOIN Orders o ... WHERE o.amount > 100 turns into an inner join, because Bob's NULL amount fails the comparison and his row is discarded. Conditions that should only restrict WHICH RIGHT ROWS MATCH belong in the ON clause (ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.amount > 100); conditions meant to filter the final combined rows belong in WHERE. For INNER JOIN the two placements give identical results — for LEFT JOIN they are different queries. Also: once two tables are in play, qualify columns (c.name, o.amount) and alias every table; ambiguous column names are errors waiting to happen.

examples.description: From Employees (id, name, department_id) and Departments (id, dept_name), show each employee with their department's name.
examples.query:
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name
FROM Employees e
INNER JOIN Departments d
  ON e.department_id = d.id;
examples.explanation: For each employee row, the engine finds the Departments row whose id equals that employee's department_id and glues the two together — the ON condition is the matching rule, and equality on a foreign-key/primary-key pair is the standard case. Because the key is Departments' PRIMARY key, each employee matches at most one department, so the row count stays 'one per employee'... except employees whose department_id matches nothing (or is NULL) are silently DROPPED — that is INNER JOIN's defining behavior, and whether that drop is acceptable is the first thing to check.

examples.description: LeetCode 175 (Combine Two Tables): from Person (personId, firstName, lastName) and Address (addressId, personId, city, state), report every person's name with city and state — people WITHOUT an address must still appear.
examples.query:
SELECT p.firstName, p.lastName, a.city, a.state
FROM Person p
LEFT JOIN Address a
  ON p.personId = a.personId;
examples.explanation: The requirement 'every person, even without an address' is precisely what LEFT JOIN guarantees: persons with a matching Address row get real city/state values, persons without one still emit a row with city and state as NULL — which the grader expects verbatim. An INNER JOIN would delete address-less people and fail. This problem exists to teach the decision procedure: the phrase 'must appear regardless' names the LEFT table, and the optional data goes on the right.

examples.description: LeetCode 183 (Customers Who Never Order): from Customers (id, name) and Orders (id, customerId), find customers with zero orders, using the NULL-padding trick.
examples.query:
SELECT c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
  ON c.id = o.customerId
WHERE o.customerId IS NULL;
examples.explanation: The LEFT JOIN outputs every customer: those with orders paired to each order, and those without orders padded with NULL in every Orders column. The WHERE then keeps ONLY the padded rows — o.customerId can be NULL only when no order matched, because in a genuine match it equals c.id, which is never NULL. The result is exactly the no-order customers. This 'LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right-key IS NULL' idiom is the join-flavored anti-join; the same answer can be written as NOT IN (with the NULL caveat from lesson 3) or NOT EXISTS, and comparing the three is a favorite interview follow-up.

examples.description: The ON vs WHERE trap, both versions shown: every customer alongside their BIG orders (amount > 100) — customers with no big orders must still be listed.
examples.query:
-- CORRECT: filter inside ON keeps all customers
SELECT c.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
  ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.amount > 100;
-- WRONG for this goal: WHERE o.amount > 100 would drop no-big-order customers entirely
examples.explanation: Putting o.amount > 100 in the ON clause changes what COUNTS AS A MATCH: small orders simply fail to match, so a customer with only small orders matches nothing and — thanks to LEFT JOIN — still appears once, NULL-padded. Moving that same predicate to WHERE instead filters the COMBINED rows after the join, where the NULL-padded customer rows have a NULL amount, NULL > 100 is UNKNOWN, and those customers vanish — silently converting your LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. Same predicate, two placements, two different queries. The rule: ON decides matching, WHERE decides survival; with LEFT JOIN, right-table filters almost always belong in ON.

examples.description: LEFT JOIN feeding GROUP BY: count each customer's orders, where never-ordered customers must show 0 (not disappear).
examples.query:
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
  ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
examples.explanation: The LEFT JOIN guarantees every customer contributes at least one row to the grouping — order-less customers contribute their single NULL-padded row. The counting must then be COUNT(o.order_id), NOT COUNT(*): COUNT(o.order_id) skips NULLs, so the padded row counts as 0 orders, while COUNT(*) would count the padded row itself and report 1. This LEFT JOIN + COUNT(right-column) pairing is the standard 'include the zeroes' aggregation pattern, and the COUNT(*) off-by-one inside it is among the most common wrong answers on join-plus-aggregate problems. Grouping by both id and name is safe because id is unique, making name constant within each bucket.

title: 8. JOINs Part 2: Self Joins, CROSS JOIN & Multi-Table Joins
summary:
A self join is not new syntax — it is an ordinary join where BOTH sides happen to be the same table, listed twice under two different aliases. The mental model: pretend you photocopied the table; Employees e JOIN Employees m compares rows of copy 'e' against rows of copy 'm'. The aliases are mandatory (otherwise every column name is ambiguous) and each alias should be named for the ROLE it plays: e for the employee, m for the manager. Self joins answer questions that compare rows of a table WITH OTHER ROWS of the same table: an employee vs. their manager (the manager_id in one row is the id of another row), today's weather vs. yesterday's, one user vs. another user with the same email. Whenever a question says 'compared to another row', think self join.

CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product: EVERY row of A paired with EVERY row of B, no ON clause, size |A| x |B|. That sounds useless until you need to GENERATE all combinations that SHOULD exist — all (student, subject) pairs so you can then count how many exams actually happened, including zeroes. The pattern 'CROSS JOIN to build the full grid, then LEFT JOIN the facts onto it' solves every 'show zero for missing combinations' problem. Accidental cross joins (forgetting a join condition) are also the classic row-explosion bug — if your result has suspiciously many rows, look for a missing ON.

Multi-table joins chain naturally: A JOIN B ON ... JOIN C ON ... — logically, A joins B first, and that combined result joins C. Each new table needs its own ON condition tying it to something already in the chain. Two habits keep big joins correct: qualify every column with its alias, and keep LEFT JOINs LEFT all the way down — if you LEFT JOIN B but then INNER JOIN C on a B column, the NULL-padded rows fail C's ON condition and are dropped, un-doing your LEFT JOIN one table later. Mixed chains of LEFT after LEFT preserve the 'keep everything from the anchor table' guarantee that problems like Students and Examinations rely on.

examples.description: LeetCode 181 (Employees Earning More Than Their Managers): from Employee (id, name, salary, managerId), find employees paid more than their manager.
examples.query:
SELECT e.name AS Employee
FROM Employee e
INNER JOIN Employee m
  ON e.managerId = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
examples.explanation: The table is used twice: alias e supplies the employee rows, alias m supplies the SAME table read as managers. The ON condition e.managerId = m.id pairs each employee with the row describing their manager — this works because managerId is a foreign key into the very same table, so following it is just a join that loops back. Once paired, both salaries sit on ONE combined row, and the WHERE compares them like any two columns. Employees with NULL managerId (the CEO) match nothing and drop out via the INNER JOIN — correct here, since 'more than their manager' is undefined without one.

examples.description: LeetCode 197 (Rising Temperature): from Weather (id, recordDate, temperature), find days warmer than the PREVIOUS day — a self join between consecutive dates.
examples.query:
SELECT today.id
FROM Weather today
INNER JOIN Weather yesterday
  ON DATEDIFF(today.recordDate, yesterday.recordDate) = 1
WHERE today.temperature > yesterday.temperature;
examples.explanation: Each row must be compared with a DIFFERENT row of the same table — the one dated exactly one day earlier — so the join condition is not key equality but a date relationship: DATEDIFF(a, b) = 1 pairs each day with its predecessor. DATEDIFF is essential; the tempting ON today.id = yesterday.id + 1 is wrong because ids are not promised to follow date order, and today.recordDate = yesterday.recordDate + 1 breaks across month boundaries under naive arithmetic. Days with no previous-day row (the first day) match nothing and are correctly excluded by the INNER JOIN, since 'warmer than yesterday' cannot be evaluated for them.

examples.description: CROSS JOIN generating a grid: from Students (student_id, student_name) and Subjects (subject_name), list every student paired with every subject — the set of exams that COULD be taken.
examples.query:
SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name
FROM Students s
CROSS JOIN Subjects sub
ORDER BY s.student_id, sub.subject_name;
examples.explanation: With no ON clause, every one of the |Students| rows pairs with every one of the |Subjects| rows: 3 students x 4 subjects = 12 rows, by construction covering every combination exactly once. This works because a cross join is what a join IS before an ON condition filters it — here we WANT the unfiltered product, because the goal is the complete grid of possibilities, including combinations for which no real data exists yet. On its own this looks academic; its power appears the moment you LEFT JOIN real events onto the grid, as the next example does.

examples.description: LeetCode 1280 (Students and Examinations): using Students, Subjects, and Examinations (student_id, subject_name), count each student's exams in EACH subject — showing 0 where they took none.
examples.query:
SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name,
       COUNT(e.subject_name) AS attended_exams
FROM Students s
CROSS JOIN Subjects sub
LEFT JOIN Examinations e
  ON e.student_id = s.student_id
 AND e.subject_name = sub.subject_name
GROUP BY s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name
ORDER BY s.student_id, sub.subject_name;
examples.explanation: Three join stages, each doing one job. The CROSS JOIN builds the full (student, subject) grid, guaranteeing a row exists for every combination — the only way 'zero exams' can appear in the output, since you cannot count rows that were never generated. The LEFT JOIN then attaches actual exam records to grid cells, on BOTH keys (student AND subject); cells with no exams stay NULL-padded rather than disappearing. Finally GROUP BY per grid cell with COUNT(e.subject_name) — counting a right-table column so NULL padding counts as 0, the lesson-7 trick. An INNER JOIN anywhere in this chain would delete the zero rows and fail the test; this grid-then-facts-then-count pipeline is THE template for 'report zeroes for missing combinations'.

examples.description: A three-table chain: from Orders (order_id, customer_id, product_id), Customers (customer_id, name), and Products (product_id, product_name, price), list each order with the customer's name and the product's name.
examples.query:
SELECT o.order_id, c.name AS customer_name, p.product_name, p.price
FROM Orders o
INNER JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
INNER JOIN Products  p ON o.product_id  = p.product_id;
examples.explanation: The chain resolves left to right: Orders joins Customers first (each order finds its buyer), and that combined result joins Products (each order also finds its item). It works because each ON clause ties the NEW table to a key already present in the running result — Orders carries both foreign keys, acting as the hub between the two dimension tables. Both joins land on primary keys, so the row count stays one-per-order, which is worth consciously verifying in any multi-join: if the count grew, some ON condition matched multiple rows. Note also what INNER means here — an order with a customer_id matching no customer would vanish; if orders must never be dropped, both joins should become LEFT with Orders as the anchor.

examples.description: Self join for duplicates with different ids: from a Person table (id, email), find pairs proving an email is duplicated — the idea behind deleting duplicates in LeetCode 196.
examples.query:
SELECT p1.id AS keep_id, p2.id AS dup_id, p1.email
FROM Person p1
INNER JOIN Person p2
  ON p1.email = p2.email
 AND p1.id < p2.id;
examples.explanation: Joining the table to itself on email equality pairs every row with every OTHER row sharing its email — but also with itself, and with each partner twice (A,B and B,A). The extra condition p1.id < p2.id kills both problems at once: a row cannot pair with itself (id < id is false), and of each (A,B)/(B,A) mirror pair only one ordering survives. This '< on the key' trick is the standard way to enumerate unordered pairs in SQL. It also directly powers dedup-deletion: every p2.id in the result has a smaller-id twin with the same email, so the p2 side is exactly the set of rows LeetCode 196's DELETE must remove — DELETE p2 FROM Person p1 JOIN Person p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id < p2.id keeps only the earliest id per email, because a row survives precisely when no same-email row with a smaller id exists to pair against it.

title: 9. Subqueries: Scalar, IN, EXISTS & Correlated
summary:
A subquery is a query nested inside another query, and it is the first tool that lets SQL answer two-step questions in one statement: 'find the average salary, THEN show everyone above it.' For simple (non-correlated) subqueries the mental model is inside-out: the inner query runs first, produces a value or a list, and the outer query treats that result like a constant it can compare against.

You must recognize four shapes instantly. A SCALAR subquery returns exactly one value (one row, one column) and can sit anywhere a value can — most often on the right side of a comparison in WHERE. An IN subquery returns a one-column list, and an outer row matches if its value appears anywhere in that list. EXISTS asks a pure yes/no question — 'does at least one matching row exist?' — and the database can stop scanning the moment it finds one. A CORRELATED subquery references a column from the outer query, so it cannot be computed once up front: conceptually it re-runs for every outer row, exactly like an inner loop inside an outer loop.

Classic mistakes: comparing with = against a subquery that can return multiple rows (MySQL error: 'Subquery returns more than 1 row' — use IN or add an aggregate so it is truly scalar); and the infamous NOT IN + NULL trap — if the inner list contains even one NULL, NOT IN returns ZERO rows, because 'x <> NULL' evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE, and one UNKNOWN in an AND-chain poisons the whole condition. Whenever the inner column can be NULL, reach for NOT EXISTS instead. On LeetCode, subqueries power a huge share of problems: above-average filters, customers who never ordered, per-department maximums, and Nth-highest values.

examples.description: Table Employees(id, name, salary). Show every employee earning more than the company-wide average salary.
examples.explanation: You cannot write WHERE salary > AVG(salary) directly, because WHERE is evaluated row by row while AVG needs to see the whole table — the two live at different stages of query execution. The scalar subquery resolves that tension: the inner query runs first and collapses the entire table into a single number (say 62000), and the outer WHERE then compares each row's salary against that constant. It works precisely because AVG over a whole table is guaranteed to return exactly one row and one column, which is what a comparison operator requires.

examples.description: Tables Customers(id, name) and Orders(id, customerId). List customers who have placed at least one order.
examples.explanation: The inner query produces the list of every customerId that appears in Orders; the outer query keeps a customer only if their id is a member of that list. This works better than a plain JOIN for a pure 'does it exist?' question: a JOIN would output one row per matching order (a customer with 5 orders appears 5 times, forcing you to add DISTINCT), whereas IN is a membership test — each customer is evaluated once, so duplicates in Orders can never inflate the result.

examples.description: Same Customers and Orders tables, but Orders.customerId can be NULL (guest checkouts). Find customers who NEVER ordered — the 'Customers Who Never Order' pattern done NULL-safely.
examples.query:
SELECT c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM Orders o
    WHERE o.customerId = c.id
);
examples.explanation: The tempting NOT IN (SELECT customerId FROM Orders) silently breaks here: if any customerId is NULL, then 'c.id NOT IN (7, NULL)' expands to 'c.id <> 7 AND c.id <> NULL', and 'c.id <> NULL' is UNKNOWN — so the whole AND-chain can never be TRUE and the query returns no rows at all. NOT EXISTS sidesteps this because it never compares against the NULL rows' values; it only asks whether at least one row satisfies o.customerId = c.id, and a NULL customerId simply fails that equality and is ignored. The SELECT 1 inside is a convention: EXISTS only cares whether a row comes back, never what is in it.

examples.description: Table Employees(id, name, salary, departmentId). Show employees who earn more than the average salary of THEIR OWN department (correlated subquery).
examples.query:
SELECT e.name, e.salary
FROM Employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
    SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
    FROM Employees e2
    WHERE e2.departmentId = e.departmentId
);
examples.explanation: The inner query mentions e.departmentId — a column of the OUTER row — so it cannot run once up front; it is logically re-evaluated for every employee, each time averaging only that employee's department. This is the inner-loop mental model: outer loop walks employees, inner loop recomputes the relevant average. It works because the correlation condition e2.departmentId = e.departmentId shrinks the aggregate's scope from 'whole company' to 'this row's group', which a plain scalar subquery could never express. (The optimizer often rewrites this into a join for speed, but you should reason about it as a per-row loop.)

examples.description: Tables Employee(id, name, salary, departmentId) and Department(id, name). For each department, return the employee(s) with the highest salary — LeetCode 'Department Highest Salary'.
examples.query:
SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id
WHERE (e.departmentId, e.salary) IN (
    SELECT departmentId, MAX(salary)
    FROM Employee
    GROUP BY departmentId
);
examples.explanation: The subquery builds one (department, top-salary) pair per department, and the outer query keeps a row only when its OWN (departmentId, salary) pair matches one of them — this multi-column IN is called a row-constructor comparison. It works because matching on the pair, not just the salary, prevents a cross-department accident: an employee earning 90000 in Sales must not qualify just because 90000 is the maximum in Engineering. A bonus over ROW_NUMBER-style solutions: if two people tie for the department maximum, both pairs match and both are returned, which is exactly what the problem wants.

examples.description: Table Employee(id, salary). Return the second-highest DISTINCT salary, or NULL if it does not exist — LeetCode 'Second Highest Salary'.
examples.explanation: The inner query finds the single highest salary; the outer WHERE throws away every row at that peak, so the MAX of what remains is by definition the second-highest distinct value — duplicates of the top salary are all excluded by the strict '<', which is why ties at the top cannot fool it. The subtle interview point is the NULL requirement: if only one distinct salary exists, the filtered set is empty and MAX over an empty set returns NULL as a value, exactly what the problem demands. A LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 approach would instead return zero rows, which LeetCode marks wrong unless you wrap it in another SELECT.

title: 10. CTEs (WITH): Readable Multi-Step Queries
summary:
A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named, temporary result set that lives only for the duration of one statement. You declare it with WITH name AS (subquery) and then use 'name' below as if it were a real table. The mental model: CTEs are variables for queries. Instead of burying a subquery three levels deep inside FROM, you name each logical step and read the statement top-to-bottom like a short program — step 1 computes monthly totals, step 2 adds a comparison, step 3 selects the answer.

Mechanically a CTE behaves like an inline view: it is not stored, not indexed, and (in MySQL) usually merged or materialized on the fly by the optimizer. You write WITH exactly once, then separate additional CTEs with commas — 'WITH a AS (...), b AS (...)' — and each later CTE may reference the earlier ones, which is what makes clean multi-step pipelines possible. A CTE can also be referenced multiple times in the final query, unlike a copy-pasted subquery.

Two reasons CTEs are essential for LeetCode. First, window functions cannot appear in WHERE (they are computed after WHERE, so at filter time the value does not exist yet); the standard fix is to compute the window column inside a CTE and filter it in the outer query, where it has become an ordinary column. Second, MySQL 8 supports WITH RECURSIVE, which can generate rows that do not exist in any table — sequences of numbers or calendars of dates — the key to 'report every day even when nothing happened' problems.

Classic mistakes: repeating the WITH keyword before every CTE instead of using commas; assuming the CTE persists across statements (it vanishes immediately); and forgetting that a recursive CTE needs a terminating WHERE in its recursive half, or it runs until the recursion depth limit kills it.

examples.description: Table Employees(id, name, salary, departmentId). Use a minimal CTE to name a filtered set before selecting from it.
examples.query:
WITH high_paid AS (
    SELECT id, name, salary
    FROM Employees
    WHERE salary > 100000
)
SELECT name, salary
FROM high_paid
ORDER BY salary DESC;
examples.explanation: This is exactly equivalent to putting the subquery inside FROM, but the intermediate result now has a NAME, which is the whole point: the reader learns the intent ('these are the high-paid people') before seeing what is done with them. It works because a CTE is just an inline view — the final SELECT treats high_paid as a table whose columns are whatever the CTE's SELECT produced. Building this habit on trivial queries pays off when queries grow to three or four steps.

examples.description: Table Employees(id, name, salary, departmentId). Show each employee next to their department's average, keeping only those above it — the 'aggregate, then rejoin' pattern.
examples.query:
WITH dept_avg AS (
    SELECT departmentId, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
    FROM Employees
    GROUP BY departmentId
)
SELECT e.name, e.salary, ROUND(d.avg_salary, 2) AS dept_average
FROM Employees e
JOIN dept_avg d ON e.departmentId = d.departmentId
WHERE e.salary > d.avg_salary;
examples.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows, so an aggregate query loses the individual employees — you cannot show a row-level salary and a group-level average in one plain SELECT. The CTE resolves this by computing the collapsed per-department numbers first, then JOINing them back onto the detail rows, so every employee row gets its department's average attached as a normal column. This 'aggregate in a CTE, join back to the base table' shape replaces a correlated subquery with something the optimizer computes once per department instead of once per employee, and it reads far better.

examples.description: Table Orders(orderId, customerId, orderDate, amount). Return each customer's single most recent order — a window function filtered through a CTE.
examples.query:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT customerId, orderId, orderDate, amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customerId ORDER BY orderDate DESC) AS rn
    FROM Orders
)
SELECT customerId, orderId, orderDate, amount
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
examples.explanation: You cannot write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() ... = 1 directly: WHERE runs BEFORE window functions are computed, so at filtering time rn does not exist yet — MySQL rejects it. The CTE creates a new query scope where the window's output has already been materialized into an ordinary column named rn, and the outer WHERE can filter it like any other value. This CTE-then-filter shape is the single most reused template in MAANG SQL interviews; memorize it as one unit.

examples.description: Table Payments(paymentId, paidAt DATETIME, amount). Chain two CTEs: bucket revenue by month, then compare each month with the previous one.
examples.query:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(paidAt, '%Y-%m') AS ym, SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM Payments
    GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(paidAt, '%Y-%m')
),
with_prev AS (
    SELECT ym, revenue,
           LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY ym) AS prev_revenue
    FROM monthly
)
SELECT ym, revenue, revenue - prev_revenue AS growth
FROM with_prev
WHERE prev_revenue IS NOT NULL;
examples.explanation: Each CTE consumes the previous one, so the statement reads as a pipeline: raw payments -> monthly totals -> monthly totals annotated with last month's figure -> growth. It works because later CTEs in the same WITH clause are allowed to reference earlier ones (note the single WITH and the comma — writing WITH twice is a syntax error). Trying to express this as nested subqueries produces the same result but forces the reader to parse it inside-out; interviews reward the version whose steps are named.

examples.description: No source table at all: generate the numbers 1 through 10 with a recursive CTE — the building block for filling gaps in sequences and calendars.
examples.explanation: A recursive CTE has two halves glued by UNION ALL: the anchor (SELECT 1) seeds the result with one row, and the recursive member (SELECT n + 1 FROM seq) repeatedly runs against the rows produced in the previous round, adding n=2, then 3, and so on. It terminates because WHERE n < 10 eventually returns no new rows — omit that guard and MySQL aborts at its recursion depth limit. This matters on LeetCode because tables only contain events that HAPPENED; when a report must show every date or id in a range, including empty ones, you generate the full range this way and LEFT JOIN the real data onto it.

title: 11. Window Functions Part 1: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK (crucial for MAANG)
summary:
Window functions are the sharpest dividing line between beginner SQL and interview SQL. The core idea: GROUP BY collapses rows into one summary row per group, but a window function ANNOTATES — every original row survives, and a new column appears whose value was computed by looking at a 'window' of related rows. The syntax is function() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...): PARTITION BY splits rows into independent groups (like GROUP BY, but without collapsing), and ORDER BY defines the ordering inside each partition that the function walks.

The three ranking functions differ only in how they treat ties, and interviewers love probing exactly that. Given scores 100, 90, 90, 80: ROW_NUMBER assigns 1,2,3,4 — always unique, ties broken arbitrarily unless you add tie-breaker columns to ORDER BY. RANK assigns 1,2,2,4 — ties share a rank and the next rank SKIPS (Olympic-style: two silvers, no bronze). DENSE_RANK assigns 1,2,2,3 — ties share and nothing is skipped. Choosing the wrong one is the most common way to fail a 'top N per group' question: ROW_NUMBER when you want exactly one row per group, DENSE_RANK when 'top 3' means 'top 3 distinct values, ties included'.

The classic mechanical mistake: window functions cannot appear in WHERE or HAVING, because they are evaluated after those clauses in the logical order of execution — at filter time the rank simply does not exist yet. The universal fix is to compute the rank inside a CTE or derived table, then filter the now-ordinary column outside. Burn the shape 'WITH ranked AS (... ROW_NUMBER() OVER ... AS rn ...) SELECT ... WHERE rn = 1' into memory; a large fraction of the LeetCode Top SQL 50 reduces to it.

examples.description: Table Employees(id, name, salary). Number all employees from highest to lowest salary — the simplest possible window.
examples.explanation: There is no PARTITION BY, so the window is the entire table: MySQL sorts all rows by salary descending and hands out 1, 2, 3... in that order. Notice what did NOT happen — no rows were merged or removed; every employee is still present, each carrying one extra computed column. That is the essential contrast with GROUP BY, and it is why window functions can answer 'show each row AND its position among its peers' questions that aggregation alone cannot.

examples.description: Table Scores(id, score). Rank scores with no gaps after ties — LeetCode 'Rank Scores', the canonical DENSE_RANK problem.
examples.query:
SELECT score,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS 'rank'
FROM Scores
ORDER BY score DESC;
examples.explanation: With scores 4.00, 4.00, 3.85, RANK would produce 1,1,3 — position 2 vanishes because RANK counts rows, not values. The problem explicitly demands 'no holes between ranks', which is the literal definition of DENSE_RANK: equal scores share a rank, and the next distinct score gets exactly the next integer. This works because DENSE_RANK increments once per new VALUE while RANK increments once per ROW consumed. Side note: rank is a reserved word in MySQL 8, so the output alias must be quoted.

examples.description: Table Orders(orderId, customerId, orderDate, amount). Return each customer's most recent order — PARTITION BY in action.
examples.query:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT customerId, orderId, orderDate, amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customerId ORDER BY orderDate DESC, orderId DESC) AS rn
    FROM Orders
)
SELECT customerId, orderId, orderDate, amount
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
examples.explanation: PARTITION BY customerId makes the numbering restart at 1 for every customer, and ORDER BY orderDate DESC guarantees that rn = 1 is that customer's newest order — so filtering rn = 1 keeps exactly one row per customer. ROW_NUMBER is the right choice over RANK precisely because we want ONE row even if two orders share a date; the extra tie-breaker orderId DESC makes the choice deterministic instead of leaving it to chance. The CTE wrapper is mandatory: WHERE cannot see rn because windows are computed after filtering.

examples.description: Tables Employee(id, name, salary, departmentId) and Department(id, name). Return the top-three UNIQUE salaries per department, ties included — LeetCode 'Department Top Three Salaries' (Hard).
examples.query:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary, e.departmentId,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.departmentId ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rk
    FROM Employee e
)
SELECT d.name AS Department, r.Employee, r.Salary
FROM ranked r
JOIN Department d ON r.departmentId = d.id
WHERE r.rk <= 3;
examples.explanation: The problem defines 'top three salaries' as the three highest DISTINCT salary values, and everyone earning any of them qualifies. DENSE_RANK encodes that definition directly: salaries 90,90,80,70,60 rank as 1,1,2,3,4, so rk <= 3 keeps both 90s plus the 80 and the 70 — five people may appear, and that is correct. ROW_NUMBER would wrongly cap the output at three rows per department, and RANK would wrongly skip values after ties (1,1,3,4 — the 70 would be rank 4 and get cut). Picking the ranking function by matching its tie behavior to the problem's wording is the entire skill being tested.

examples.description: Table Employee(id, salary). Return the Nth highest distinct salary (say N = 2), NULL if absent — the ranking alternative to LIMIT/OFFSET.
examples.query:
SELECT MAX(salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM (
    SELECT salary,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk
    FROM Employee
) t
WHERE rk = 2;
examples.explanation: DENSE_RANK over distinct-aware ordering makes rk = N mean 'the Nth highest distinct value' even when duplicates exist — with salaries 300,300,200, LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 on the raw rows returns 300 again (wrong), while DENSE_RANK gives 300 rank 1 and 200 rank 2 (right). Wrapping the filter in MAX() handles the missing case elegantly: if no row has rk = 2, MAX over the empty set yields NULL as a value instead of an empty result, which is what LeetCode's judge expects. This N-as-a-parameter shape generalizes to any 'Nth highest' variant.

title: 12. Window Functions Part 2: LAG, LEAD, Running Totals & Moving Averages (frames ROWS BETWEEN)
summary:
Part 1 ranked rows; this part lets a row LOOK AT ITS NEIGHBORS. LAG(col) OVER (ORDER BY ...) fetches the value of col from the previous row in the window's order, LEAD fetches from the next row, and both accept an offset and a default: LAG(col, 2, 0) means 'two rows back, or 0 if that runs off the edge' (without a default you get NULL at the boundary). The mental model: after sorting, each row grows a little periscope aimed backward or forward. Any 'compare today with yesterday', 'did the price rise', or 'find consecutive...' problem is a LAG/LEAD problem.

The second superpower is running aggregates: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY orderDate) turns a plain sum into a cumulative total that grows row by row. What controls exactly WHICH rows feed each row's aggregate is the FRAME, written like ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — 'this row plus the six before it', i.e. a sliding 7-row window, the standard shape for moving averages.

Two classic traps. First, the default frame: when you write ORDER BY but no explicit frame, MySQL uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and RANGE treats rows that tie on the ORDER BY key as one block — two orders on the same date both show the total INCLUDING each other, which quietly corrupts running totals. Write ROWS explicitly whenever ties are possible. Second, LAG moves one ROW back, not one DAY back: if dates have gaps, the previous row might be from last week, so 'compare with yesterday' problems must also verify the date distance (e.g. with DATEDIFF = 1). Finally, remember that a moving average near the start of the data has an incomplete window — decide explicitly whether those rows should be excluded, as LeetCode's Restaurant Growth does.

examples.description: Table Weather(id, recordDate, temperature). Show each day's temperature next to the previous day's — the simplest LAG.
examples.explanation: ORDER BY recordDate inside OVER defines the timeline, and LAG simply copies temperature from the row one step earlier on that timeline into the current row. The first row has no predecessor, so its prev_temperature is NULL — LAG's polite way of saying 'off the edge'. This works because the window's ORDER BY is what gives 'previous' a meaning at all; without it, table rows have no reliable order and 'the previous row' is undefined.

examples.description: Table Weather(id, recordDate, temperature). Return ids of days warmer than the PREVIOUS CALENDAR DAY — LeetCode 'Rising Temperature' via LAG, with the date-gap trap handled.
examples.query:
WITH w AS (
    SELECT id, recordDate, temperature,
           LAG(temperature) OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_temp,
           LAG(recordDate)  OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_date
    FROM Weather
)
SELECT id
FROM w
WHERE temperature > prev_temp
  AND DATEDIFF(recordDate, prev_date) = 1;
examples.explanation: LAG gives the previous ROW, and rows are not guaranteed to be consecutive days — if the table skips a day, the previous row is two or more days old and must not count. Pulling BOTH lagged columns lets the outer query check the two conditions the problem actually states: warmer (temperature > prev_temp) and truly adjacent (DATEDIFF = 1). Rows where prev_temp is NULL (the first day) fail the comparison automatically because NULL comparisons are never TRUE, which conveniently excludes the boundary without extra code. This 'lag the value AND lag the key, then validate the gap' pattern recurs in every consecutive-events problem.

examples.description: Table Orders(orderId, orderDate, amount), one order per day. Compute cumulative revenue over time — a running total.
examples.explanation: Adding ORDER BY to an aggregate window changes its meaning from 'total of everything' to 'total of everything up to me': each row sums the frame that starts at the first row and ends at itself. The explicit ROWS clause is deliberate defensive style — the implicit default is RANGE, and under RANGE two rows tying on orderDate would each include the other's amount, showing the same inflated total on both. Spelling out ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW makes the frame count physical rows, which is almost always what a running total means.

examples.description: Table Customer(customer_id, visited_on, amount), daily totals. Report the 7-day moving sum and average of spending, only for days with a full 7-day window — LeetCode 'Restaurant Growth'.
examples.query:
WITH daily AS (
    SELECT visited_on, SUM(amount) AS day_amount
    FROM Customer
    GROUP BY visited_on
),
windowed AS (
    SELECT visited_on,
           SUM(day_amount) OVER (ORDER BY visited_on ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS amount,
           ROUND(AVG(day_amount) OVER (ORDER BY visited_on ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS average_amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY visited_on) AS day_no
    FROM daily
)
SELECT visited_on, amount, average_amount
FROM windowed
WHERE day_no >= 7;
examples.explanation: Three ideas stack here. The first CTE collapses multiple customers per day into one row per day, because the frame counts ROWS and would otherwise slide over customers instead of days. ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW then makes every aggregate see exactly this day plus the six before it — a true 7-day window once each row IS a day. Finally, the first six days have fewer than seven rows behind them, so their 'average' would be over a short window; ROW_NUMBER tags each day's position and the outer filter day_no >= 7 keeps only complete windows, which is precisely what the problem demands. Note the filter must live OUTSIDE the CTE — the windows must be computed over all days first, then trimmed.

examples.description: Table Logs(id, num) with consecutive ids. Find all numbers appearing at least three times in a row — LeetCode 'Consecutive Numbers' via LAG with offset.
examples.query:
SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM (
    SELECT num,
           LAG(num, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev1,
           LAG(num, 2) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev2
    FROM Logs
) t
WHERE num = prev1 AND num = prev2;
examples.explanation: A number appears three times consecutively exactly when some row equals both the row 1 back and the row 2 back — LAG's offset argument reaches those directly, so the run-of-three condition becomes two simple equalities on one row. Ordering by id is what defines 'consecutive' here. The first two rows get NULLs from LAG and fail the equality harmlessly. DISTINCT is essential and often forgotten: a run of five equal values satisfies the condition at three different rows, and without DISTINCT the same num would be reported three times.

title: 13. CASE WHEN: Conditional Logic & Pivoting
summary:
CASE is SQL's if/else — but crucially it is an EXPRESSION, not a statement: it produces a value, so it can sit anywhere a value can — in SELECT to compute a column, inside SUM() or COUNT(), in ORDER BY to customize sorting, even in an UPDATE's SET. It evaluates its WHEN conditions top to bottom and returns the THEN of the FIRST one that is true; nothing after the first match is even looked at, so you can (and should) order conditions from most to least specific. If no condition matches and there is no ELSE, the result is NULL — a silent default that either bites you or, as you will see, becomes a feature.

The skill that separates interview candidates is CONDITIONAL AGGREGATION: putting CASE inside an aggregate. SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) totals only approved rows while the query as a whole still sees every row.
