This is how you compute several differently-filtered numbers side by side in ONE pass — a WHERE clause could only apply one filter to the whole query. Push it further and you get PIVOTING: one CASE-aggregate per target column turns rows ('Jan', 'Feb'...) into columns (Jan_Revenue, Feb_Revenue), with GROUP BY collapsing each entity to a single wide row.

Classic mistakes: COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts EVERY row, because COUNT counts non-NULL values and 0 is not NULL — either drop the ELSE (so misses become NULL and are skipped) or use SUM with ELSE 0. Also remember MySQL's shortcut: a boolean expression is already 1 or 0, so SUM(state = 'approved') works — concise, but say the CASE version in interviews for portability. Finally, watch NULL handling: WHEN score >= 60 puts NULL scores into the ELSE bucket silently, which may or may not be what you meant.

examples.description: Table Products(id, name, price). Add a human-readable price tier to every product.
examples.query:
SELECT name, price,
       CASE
           WHEN price < 20 THEN 'budget'
           WHEN price < 100 THEN 'standard'
           ELSE 'premium'
       END AS tier
FROM Products;
examples.explanation: Conditions run top to bottom and stop at the first hit, which is why 'WHEN price < 100' does not need to say 'AND price >= 20' — anything under 20 was already captured by the first branch and never reaches the second. The ELSE catches everything else, including any NULL price (a NULL fails both comparisons); if you want NULLs labeled separately, you must add 'WHEN price IS NULL' as an explicit first branch. This top-down short-circuit is the core mental model for every CASE you will ever write.

examples.description: Table Triangle(x, y, z), three segment lengths per row. Decide whether each row can form a triangle — LeetCode 'Triangle Judgement'.
examples.query:
SELECT x, y, z,
       CASE
           WHEN x + y > z AND x + z > y AND y + z > x THEN 'Yes'
           ELSE 'No'
       END AS triangle
FROM Triangle;
examples.explanation: The triangle inequality must hold for ALL three pairings, so the WHEN joins the three checks with AND — a common bug is testing only x + y > z, which wrongly accepts rows where a different side is too long. CASE fits this problem better than filtering because the task is to LABEL every row, not remove any: WHERE would drop the 'No' rows, while CASE keeps all rows and computes a verdict per row. This 'classify, do not filter' distinction tells you instantly whether a problem wants WHERE or CASE.

examples.description: Table Transactions(id, country, state, amount, trans_date). For each month and country, count total vs approved transactions in one pass — conditional aggregation (LeetCode 'Monthly Transactions I' core).
examples.query:
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(trans_date, '%Y-%m') AS month, country,
       COUNT(*) AS trans_count,
       SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS approved_count,
       SUM(amount) AS trans_total_amount,
       SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS approved_total_amount
FROM Transactions
GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(trans_date, '%Y-%m'), country;
examples.explanation: The query needs BOTH all-transaction totals and approved-only totals from the same rows, so filtering with WHERE state = 'approved' is impossible — it would destroy the data the unfiltered columns need. The CASE inside each SUM applies a private, per-column filter: approved rows contribute their real value, everything else contributes 0, and the group total comes out right. This is the fundamental reason conditional aggregation exists: one shared row set, many independently filtered aggregates. Had these been COUNTs, you would drop the ELSE 0 (or keep SUM), because COUNT would happily count the zeros.

examples.description: Table Salary(id, name, sex ENUM('m','f'), salary). Flip every 'm' to 'f' and vice versa with ONE statement and no temp table — LeetCode 'Swap Salary'.
examples.query:
UPDATE Salary
SET sex = CASE WHEN sex = 'm' THEN 'f' ELSE 'm' END;
examples.explanation: The naive plan — one UPDATE to turn m into f, then another to turn f into m — self-destructs: after the first statement EVERY row is 'f', so the second flips the entire table to 'm'. A single UPDATE avoids that because SQL evaluates the CASE against each row's ORIGINAL value within one statement; there is no intermediate corrupted state for the logic to trip over. This demonstrates that CASE is an expression usable inside SET, and it is the standard interview answer for any 'swap two values in place' variation.

examples.description: Table Department(id, revenue, month) with one row per (id, month). Pivot months into columns: one row per id with Jan_Revenue, Feb_Revenue, ... — LeetCode 'Reformat Department Table' style.
examples.query:
SELECT id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'Jan' THEN revenue END) AS Jan_Revenue,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'Feb' THEN revenue END) AS Feb_Revenue,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'Mar' THEN revenue END) AS Mar_Revenue,
       SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'Apr' THEN revenue END) AS Apr_Revenue
FROM Department
GROUP BY id;
examples.explanation: Each output column owns one CASE that passes through revenue only for its month; with no ELSE, every other row yields NULL, and aggregates IGNORE NULLs — so after GROUP BY id collapses the months into one row, each column holds exactly that month's revenue (or NULL if the month never occurred, matching the expected output). The deliberate omission of ELSE is the trick: ELSE 0 would turn genuinely-missing months into 0, which is a different claim than 'no data'. MySQL has no PIVOT keyword, so this CASE-per-column + GROUP BY construction IS how pivoting is done, and MAX works in place of SUM when each (id, month) pair is unique.

title: 14. String Functions & Regular Expressions (CONCAT, UPPER/LOWER, SUBSTRING, GROUP_CONCAT, REGEXP)
summary:
String problems on LeetCode are less about cleverness and more about knowing a small toolbox cold — and its sharp edges. CONCAT(a, b, ...) glues strings, but returns NULL if ANY argument is NULL (CONCAT_WS('sep', ...) skips NULLs instead, which is why it is safer for optional middle names). UPPER and LOWER change case. SUBSTRING(str, start, len) extracts a piece — and here is the trap that bites every programmer: SQL strings are 1-INDEXED. SUBSTRING(name, 1, 1) is the first character, and SUBSTRING(name, 2) with no length means 'from position 2 to the end'. For lengths, CHAR_LENGTH counts characters while LENGTH counts BYTES — identical for ASCII, different for multibyte text like 'café', so measuring text should default to CHAR_LENGTH.

GROUP_CONCAT is the odd one out: it is an AGGREGATE that folds a whole group's values into one string, with its own internal modifiers — GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT product ORDER BY product SEPARATOR ',') deduplicates, sorts, and joins in a single call. Forgetting the internal ORDER BY is the classic way to fail a test that expects alphabetical output, because without it the order is whatever the engine happened to scan.

For matching, LIKE handles simple wildcards: % is 'any run of characters (possibly empty)' and _ is 'exactly one'. REGEXP is the power tool: character classes [a-z], repetition * and +, anchors ^ (start) and $ (end), alternation |. Two habits prevent most regex bugs: anchor your pattern when you mean 'the WHOLE string must match' (REGEXP matches anywhere inside the string by default), and escape literal dots as \. — an unescaped dot means 'any character', so '@leetcode.com' would happily accept '@leetcodeXcom'.

examples.description: Table Users(id, first_name, last_name). Build a display name in shouting caps.
examples.query:
SELECT CONCAT(UPPER(first_name), ' ', UPPER(last_name)) AS display_name
FROM Users;
examples.explanation: Functions compose inside out: each UPPER runs first, then CONCAT stitches the pieces with a space literal in the middle. The practical caveat is NULL-poisoning: if last_name is NULL, the whole CONCAT returns NULL, not 'JOHN ' — because in SQL, combining anything with NULL yields NULL. When parts are optional, CONCAT_WS(' ', first_name, last_name) is the fix, since it skips NULL arguments instead of propagating them. Knowing WHY the NULL swallows the row is what turns this from trivia into debugging skill.

examples.description: Table Users(user_id, name) with names in random case like 'aLICE'. Fix each to exactly one leading capital — LeetCode 'Fix Names in a Table'.
examples.query:
SELECT user_id,
       CONCAT(UPPER(SUBSTRING(name, 1, 1)), LOWER(SUBSTRING(name, 2))) AS name
FROM Users
ORDER BY user_id;
examples.explanation: The name is split at its 1-indexed seams: SUBSTRING(name, 1, 1) is the first character (position 1, length 1 — NOT position 0), and SUBSTRING(name, 2) with the length omitted means 'everything from position 2 onward', which elegantly handles names of any length including one-letter names, where it returns an empty string rather than an error. Uppercase the head, lowercase the tail, CONCAT them back. This works because SQL has no 'capitalize' built-in — decompose-transform-reassemble IS the idiom, and the 1-indexing is where most first attempts fail.

examples.description: Table Tweets(tweet_id, content). Find tweets STRICTLY longer than 15 characters — LeetCode 'Invalid Tweets', and the CHAR_LENGTH vs LENGTH lesson.
examples.explanation: CHAR_LENGTH counts characters, LENGTH counts bytes; for plain ASCII they agree, but a single emoji or accented letter occupies multiple bytes in UTF-8, so LENGTH('café') is 5 while CHAR_LENGTH('café') is 4. A tweet's length limit is defined in characters a human sees, so CHAR_LENGTH is the semantically correct function — and using it every time you measure text means never being burned when unicode shows up in the test data. The strict > 15 (not >= ) mirrors the problem statement exactly; off-by-one on the comparison is the other common failure here.

examples.description: Table Activities(sell_date, product), one row per sale. Per day, count distinct products and list them alphabetically comma-separated — LeetCode 'Group Sold Products By The Date' via GROUP_CONCAT.
examples.query:
SELECT sell_date,
       COUNT(DISTINCT product) AS num_sold,
       GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT product ORDER BY product SEPARATOR ',') AS products
FROM Activities
GROUP BY sell_date
ORDER BY sell_date;
examples.explanation: GROUP_CONCAT is an aggregate, so it runs once per sell_date group and folds that day's product values into one string. Each modifier earns its place: DISTINCT collapses repeat sales of the same product (matching COUNT(DISTINCT ...) so the number and the list agree), the INTERNAL ORDER BY product sorts within the string (the outer ORDER BY only sorts rows, not the contents of the string — the number-one mistake here), and SEPARATOR ',' pins the delimiter the judge expects. Without the internal ORDER BY, results are in scan order and fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure to debug.

examples.description: Table Users(user_id, name, mail). Keep only valid emails: prefix starts with a letter, then letters/digits/underscore/dot/dash, domain exactly '@leetcode.com' — LeetCode 'Find Users With Valid E-Mails'.
examples.explanation: Every piece of this pattern is a deliberate defense. The ^ and $ anchors force the ENTIRE mail to match — without them, REGEXP matches any substring, so garbage like 'xx!alice@leetcode.com' would pass because a valid-looking chunk exists inside it. '^[a-zA-Z]' pins the first character to a letter, and '[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]*' allows zero or more of the permitted characters after it (inside a character class the dot and dash are literal). Finally '\\.com' escapes the dot: an unescaped '.' means 'any single character', which would wrongly accept '@leetcode2com'. LIKE cannot express 'starts with a letter' or character sets at all, which is exactly when you escalate to REGEXP.

examples.description: Table Patients(patient_id, patient_name, conditions), conditions is a space-separated code list like 'SADIAB100 DIAB1002'. Find patients with a Type I Diabetes code, which PREFIXES with DIAB1 — LeetCode 'Patients With a Condition'.
examples.query:
SELECT patient_id, patient_name, conditions
FROM Patients
WHERE conditions LIKE 'DIAB1%'
   OR conditions LIKE '% DIAB1%';
examples.explanation: The naive LIKE '%DIAB1%' fails because it matches DIAB1 ANYWHERE, including mid-code — 'SADIAB100' contains DIAB1 but is not a Type I code. A code starts with DIAB1 only in two positions: at the very beginning of the string (LIKE 'DIAB1%') or immediately after a space separating codes (LIKE '% DIAB1%') — the leading space in the second pattern IS the word boundary. The OR covers both cases exhaustively. The same idea in one regex is REGEXP '\\bDIAB1', where \\b asserts a word boundary; either way, the transferable lesson is that substring matching over delimited lists must respect the delimiter, not just the letters.

title: 15. Date & Time Functions (DATEDIFF, DATE_ADD/SUB, DATE_FORMAT, comparisons)
summary:
Dates in MySQL are real typed values, not strings — DATE holds a calendar day, DATETIME adds a time of day — and because the type knows the calendar, ordinary comparison operators just work: orderDate >= '2026-01-01' compares chronologically, with the quoted 'YYYY-MM-DD' literal parsed into a date. That one fact unlocks most date filtering; the rest is a toolbox of four functions.

DATEDIFF(a, b) returns a minus b in whole DAYS — the argument order is the single most common date bug, so anchor the memory: DATEDIFF('2026-01-02','2026-01-01') = 1, later date first, like subtraction. DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 1 DAY) and DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL 30 DAY) shift a date by any unit (DAY, MONTH, YEAR...), and unlike DATEDIFF they respect calendars — adding a month to Jan 31 lands correctly at Feb 28/29, which handwritten day arithmetic gets wrong. DATE_FORMAT(d, '%Y-%m') renders a date as text using format codes (%Y four-digit year, %m two-digit month, %d day), and formatting to 'YYYY-MM' is THE standard trick for monthly grouping: every date in the same month produces the same string, so GROUP BY collapses months. Extractors YEAR(), MONTH(), DAY() pull numeric parts when you need them individually.

Two traps to internalize. First, an inclusive N-day window ending today starts at DATE_SUB(today, INTERVAL N-1 DAY) — 30 days means subtracting 29, because today itself is day one; off-by-one here is the classic 'User Activity for the Past 30 Days' failure. Second, mixing DATE columns with DATETIME boundaries: BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31' on a DATETIME column stops at Jan 31 00:00:00 and silently drops the rest of that day — prefer half-open ranges: col >= '2026-01-01' AND col < '2026-02-01'.

examples.description: Table Orders(orderId, customerId, orderDate DATE, amount). Pull all orders from January 2026 with a plain typed comparison.
examples.query:
SELECT orderId, orderDate, amount
FROM Orders
WHERE orderDate >= '2026-01-01'
  AND orderDate < '2026-02-01';
examples.explanation: Because orderDate is a DATE column, MySQL parses both quoted literals into dates and the comparison is truly chronological — no string tricks involved. The half-open range (>= start, < next-month-start) is deliberately chosen over BETWEEN: it captures every instant of January including a hypothetical DATETIME at '2026-01-31 23:59:59', and the same shape works unchanged for any period. It also beats WHERE DATE_FORMAT(orderDate, '%Y-%m') = '2026-01' in production, because wrapping the COLUMN in a function defeats any index on it, while a bare range comparison can use one.

examples.description: Table Weather(id, recordDate, temperature). Find ids of days warmer than the previous calendar day — LeetCode 'Rising Temperature' with a self-join and DATEDIFF.
examples.query:
SELECT w1.id
FROM Weather w1
JOIN Weather w2
  ON DATEDIFF(w1.recordDate, w2.recordDate) = 1
WHERE w1.temperature > w2.temperature;
examples.explanation: The self-join pairs every day w1 with candidate days w2, and the join condition DATEDIFF(w1.recordDate, w2.recordDate) = 1 keeps only the pair where w2 is exactly one day earlier — argument order matters: today minus yesterday must equal +1, and swapping the arguments yields -1 and an empty result, the most common wrong submission on this problem. DATEDIFF also absorbs the calendar math that a naive w1.id = w2.id + 1 would botch (ids are not guaranteed consecutive, and dates can skip days). With the right pair welded together, the WHERE simply compares the two temperatures.

examples.description: Table Activity(user_id, session_id, activity_date, activity_type). Count daily active users for the 30-day window ending 2019-07-27 inclusive — LeetCode 'User Activity for the Past 30 Days I'.
examples.query:
SELECT activity_date AS day,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users
FROM Activity
WHERE activity_date BETWEEN DATE_SUB('2019-07-27', INTERVAL 29 DAY) AND '2019-07-27'
GROUP BY activity_date;
examples.explanation: The interval subtracts 29, not 30 — that is the entire test. A 30-day window that INCLUDES its end date spans end-29 through end: count the fence posts (June 28 through July 27 is 30 distinct days), so subtracting 30 would produce a 31-day window and overcount. DATE_SUB with INTERVAL does the calendar-aware arithmetic (month lengths, year boundaries) that manual math gets wrong. COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) is the second why: a user with five sessions in one day must count once for that day, and DISTINCT inside the per-day groups delivers exactly that.

examples.description: Table Transactions(id, country, state, amount, trans_date). Report per-month, per-country transaction counts and totals — DATE_FORMAT as a grouping bucket (LeetCode 'Monthly Transactions I').
examples.query:
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(trans_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
       country,
       COUNT(*) AS trans_count,
       SUM(amount) AS trans_total_amount
FROM Transactions
GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(trans_date, '%Y-%m'), country;
examples.explanation: GROUP BY needs equal keys to merge rows, and raw dates within a month are all different — DATE_FORMAT solves this by projecting every date onto a shared label: 2019-12-03 and 2019-12-18 both become '2019-12', so the group means 'this month'. The '%Y-%m' code pair is chosen (not '%m' alone) because December 2019 and December 2020 must remain separate groups; dropping the year silently merges them, a bug that only appears once data spans years. Grouping by the same expression as the SELECT keeps the query valid under MySQL's ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode, which LeetCode runs.

examples.description: Table Activity(player_id, device_id, event_date, games_played). What fraction of players logged in the day immediately AFTER their first login? — LeetCode 'Game Play Analysis IV', DATE_ADD inside a join.
examples.query:
WITH firsts AS (
    SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_date
    FROM Activity
    GROUP BY player_id
)
SELECT ROUND(
    COUNT(a.player_id) / (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT player_id) FROM Activity),
    2
) AS fraction
FROM firsts f
LEFT JOIN Activity a
  ON a.player_id = f.player_id
 AND a.event_date = DATE_ADD(f.first_date, INTERVAL 1 DAY);
examples.explanation: Step one pins each player's first login with MIN(event_date). The LEFT JOIN then tries to find, for each player, an activity row dated EXACTLY first_date + 1 — DATE_ADD computes that target date correctly across month and year boundaries, where '+ 1' on a date column would not be portable arithmetic. The LEFT JOIN (not INNER) is the crux: players without a next-day login still produce a row with a NULL a.player_id, and COUNT(a.player_id) skips NULLs — so the numerator counts only the retained players while the denominator subquery counts everyone, giving the fraction in one pass. This 'anchor date, probe for anchor+interval' pattern powers every retention question.

title: 16. UNION, DELETE/UPDATE Patterns & LeetCode SQL Playbook
summary:
UNION stacks the results of two SELECTs vertically. The two queries must produce the same number of columns in compatible types; column names come from the FIRST select, and a trailing ORDER BY sorts the COMBINED result, not the last branch. The critical choice: UNION deduplicates the merged rows (paying a sort/hash cost to do it), UNION ALL keeps everything as-is. Default to UNION ALL and upgrade to UNION only when duplicates are actually possible and unwanted — saying that out loud in an interview signals you understand the cost. UNION also lets MySQL fake what it lacks natively: a FULL OUTER JOIN is 'LEFT JOIN result UNION rows only in the right table'.

LeetCode's write-statement problems reduce to two templates. Deleting duplicates: MySQL forbids 'DELETE FROM t WHERE ... (SELECT ... FROM t)' referencing the same table directly, so you use multi-table delete syntax — DELETE p1 FROM Person p1 JOIN Person p2 ON ... — where the alias after DELETE names WHICH table's rows die. Conditional updates: UPDATE with CASE flips values in one statement, avoiding the two-statement trap where the first update destroys the information the second needs.

Now the playbook — the handful of shapes that solve most of the Top SQL 50. Top-N per group: window rank in a CTE, filter rank outside (choose ROW_NUMBER / RANK / DENSE_RANK by the tie wording). Consecutive rows: LAG/LEAD equalities, or a self-join on id difference. Gaps and islands: id minus ROW_NUMBER() is CONSTANT within a consecutive run — group by that difference to find streaks. Dedup keeping one row: keep MIN(id) per key, delete or exclude the rest. Never-matched rows: LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL or NOT EXISTS (never NOT IN when NULLs can lurk). When you read a new problem, your first move is classifying it into one of these shapes — that classification IS the interview skill.

examples.description: Tables sales_2024(product, amount) and sales_2025(product, amount) — an archive split by year. Stack them into one result for reporting.
examples.query:
SELECT product, amount, '2024' AS sales_year FROM sales_2024
UNION ALL
SELECT product, amount, '2025' FROM sales_2025
ORDER BY sales_year, product;
examples.explanation: UNION ALL is correct here because the two tables describe DIFFERENT years — identical-looking rows (same product, same amount) in both years are two real sales, and plain UNION would silently merge them into one, corrupting totals. The added literal column tags each row with its origin, which is the standard trick to keep provenance after stacking; it must appear in both branches so column counts match. The ORDER BY at the bottom governs the combined result — to sort one branch alone you would have to wrap it in parentheses, a nuance interviewers occasionally probe.

examples.description: Tables Employees(employee_id, name) and Salaries(employee_id, salary), each possibly missing people the other has. Report every employee_id missing from EITHER table, sorted — LeetCode 'Employees With Missing Information', i.e. a faked FULL OUTER JOIN.
examples.query:
SELECT employee_id FROM Employees
WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Salaries)
UNION
SELECT employee_id FROM Salaries
WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Employees)
ORDER BY employee_id;
examples.explanation: MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN, so the two 'one-sided orphan' queries are computed separately and stacked: ids with a name but no salary, then ids with a salary but no name. UNION (not ALL) is the right variant for once — an id cannot appear in both branches here, but UNION also serves as a safety net and matches the 'report each id once' requirement. NOT IN is safe in this specific problem because employee_id is a primary key and cannot be NULL; if it were nullable, the NOT IN + NULL trap would empty the result and NOT EXISTS would be mandatory — always run that mental check before shipping NOT IN.

examples.description: Table Person(id, email) with duplicate emails. DELETE all duplicates, keeping only the row with the smallest id per email — LeetCode 'Delete Duplicate Emails'.
examples.query:
DELETE p1
FROM Person p1
JOIN Person p2
  ON p1.email = p2.email
 AND p1.id > p2.id;
examples.explanation: The self-join pairs each row p1 with every OTHER row p2 sharing its email that has a smaller id. A row finds such a partner exactly when it is NOT the minimum id of its email group — the minimal row has nobody below it, joins to nothing, and survives. 'DELETE p1' (rather than DELETE FROM Person) is the multi-table delete syntax that declares which side of the join gets deleted; it exists precisely because MySQL rejects a plain DELETE whose WHERE subqueries the same table being modified. The condition p1.id > p2.id also guarantees you can never delete the keeper by accident, because the minimum can never be on the left of a strict >.

examples.description: PLAYBOOK — Top-N per group. Table Employee(id, name, salary, departmentId): top 3 distinct salaries per department, the reusable template.
examples.query:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT name, salary, departmentId,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk
    FROM Employee
)
SELECT departmentId, name, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rk <= 3;
examples.explanation: This template is three decisions welded together, and each maps to a phrase in the problem statement. PARTITION BY is the 'per group' phrase; ORDER BY ... DESC is the 'top by what' phrase; the function choice encodes the tie policy — DENSE_RANK because 'top 3 salaries' here means three distinct VALUES with all ties included, whereas 'exactly one newest row per customer' would demand ROW_NUMBER. The CTE exists because WHERE cannot see window output (windows compute after filtering), so the rank must become an ordinary column first. Rehearse mapping problem wording onto these three slots until it is automatic — that is the entire top-N-per-group genre.

examples.description: PLAYBOOK — Consecutive rows via self-join. Table Cinema/Seat-style Logs(id, num) with ids consecutive: find numbers appearing 3+ times in a row without window functions.
examples.query:
SELECT DISTINCT l1.num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM Logs l1
JOIN Logs l2 ON l2.id = l1.id + 1 AND l2.num = l1.num
JOIN Logs l3 ON l3.id = l1.id + 2 AND l3.num = l1.num;
examples.explanation: Each join extends the chain by one physically-adjacent row required to hold the same num: l2 must sit exactly one id after l1 with an equal value, l3 exactly two after — so a surviving l1 row proves a run of three. It works only because this table guarantees ids are consecutive with no gaps; when ids can jump (deleted rows), 'adjacent' must be defined by LAG over an ORDER BY instead, which is why knowing BOTH forms matters. DISTINCT collapses long runs that would otherwise report the same num once per starting position. Compare this to the LAG version and note they express the identical idea: reach k rows away and demand equality.

examples.description: PLAYBOOK — Gaps and islands. Table Stadium(id, visit_date, people) with consecutive ids: display rows with people >= 100 belonging to a streak of 3+ consecutive ids — LeetCode 'Human Traffic of Stadium'.
examples.query:
WITH busy AS (
    SELECT id, visit_date, people,
           id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp
    FROM Stadium
    WHERE people >= 100
)
SELECT id, visit_date, people
FROM busy
WHERE grp IN (
    SELECT grp FROM busy GROUP BY grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
)
ORDER BY visit_date;
examples.explanation: The magic is the difference id - ROW_NUMBER(): after filtering to busy days, ROW_NUMBER increments by exactly 1 per kept row, and id also increments by exactly 1 while a run is unbroken — so their difference stays CONSTANT within a consecutive island and jumps when a gap appears (id skips ahead, row_number does not). Identical grp therefore means 'same streak', turning an ordering problem into a grouping problem: HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 finds islands long enough, and the outer query pulls back their member rows. This id-minus-rownumber trick is the standard weapon for every 'streak of at least N' question — attendance streaks, login streaks, sensor uptime — and recognizing it on sight is a genuine MAANG differentiator.
